kandidaty.tekst: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it.

- Added a confirmation before /install-github-app changes a repository
- Added claude mcp add-json <name> - to read the server's JSON from stdin, so tokens can stay off the command line; not available inside a Claude Code session
- Added a line when a resumed session's earlier messages can't be loaded
- Added a list in /status of broken agent, skill, command and output style files, keybinding errors, an unavailable sandbox, ignored permission settings and hook matchers that never match
- Added a note in /config when other settings override a row
- Added x-claude-code-managed-settings-checksum to the gateway hint headers; sent where managed settings set CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1, including where they already do
- Added support for naming a session's billing group with the attributionProject setting, for Claude apps gateways that set admin.billing_group_tag
- Added /tui classic as the name for the non-fullscreen renderer; /tui default still works
- [VSCode] Added "Claude Code: Add to Chat" to the Explorer's right-click menu, which @-mentions the selected files and folders in the chat
- Changed some pre-started background sessions to be discarded after an account change
- Changed a workflow paused at a usage limit in the terminal to stay paused after a login, until the earlier login returns or you type a prompt
- Bug fixes and reliability improvements
- Changed ExitWorktree to ask before removing a worktree that may hold unsaved work; refused in don't-ask mode or with nobody to answer, unless an allow rule, auto or bypass permissions mode allows it
- Changed claude mcp add --scope project to stop, instead of overwriting the file, when .mcp.json lists its servers at the top level with no mcpServers key
- Changed the arrow keys on most permission prompts to stop at No instead of wrapping around; a number past the last answer moves to No
- Changed path checks to refuse some symbolic links
- Changed what counts as inside a working directory, so some paths now ask for permission
- Changed permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories to ask about more Bash commands in bypass and auto modes, and to deny some in auto mode

kandidaty.zagolovok: External sandboxes for coding agents
kandidaty.tekst:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

- external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.

- external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.

- external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

Tags: sandboxing, security, ai, webassembly, generative-ai, llms, coding-agents, claude-code, codex, pi

kandidaty.zagolovok: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
kandidaty.tekst:
Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.

You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io:

- Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script

- Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI

- Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository

- Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette

- Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools

The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.

As an example, consider the following URL:

https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this:

That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.

Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing:

https://lite.datasette.io/
?install=datasette-maplibre
&url=https://.../demo.db
&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins.

&url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.

&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.

#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it (%23 is a URL-encoded #) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the ma

kandidaty.zagolovok: Productiv-icky
kandidaty.tekst:
productiv-icky (adj.) - the feeling of doing work you didn’t mean to do

We have a problem.

full interactive post is here

We agree this is insane, right? Someone I don’t know sends me emails that I’m expected to reply to. I don’t know them. I don’t work for them.

So I ignore them (well actually I send them to email jail). Nuh-uh, that’s not my work, buddy.

But it’s different if it’s my super-intelligent, helpful agent friend…

Yeses are easy. They’re quick.

But every yes has a yes-tax. The hidden extra work you didn’t think of. The long tail of regret where you question why you ever said yes.

Say I did reply to those emails, they’d send me stuff to read to show how great they are at their job and how much better I’d be. Then we’d organise a call (which would derail whichever day that call was on). Then we’d have follow-up items. Then a string of other crap I couldn’t care less about.

I know what’s going to happen. I can smell it, it stinks. I’ve said yes and paid the tax many times before. Now I pay $200/mo for a super-intelligent, over-eager, needy little nerd to ping me incessantly about taking things off my plate.

I feel bad for him. He wants to work. He’s gagging for it. Just. One. More. Task. Master.

Plus, my little nerd has a gambling problem. Or rather, he feeds mine.

Remember years ago sending tons of Slack messages to get the most out of your $20/mo plan? Nor me. Why? Because it’s dumb. But now we feel like we should use all our tokens before they run out. Why? Because everyone else is.

We started measuring shovels instead of the hole.

Someone’s needy little nerd booked their dentist, replied to their mum and launched a business whilst they were asleep. They’ve got an org chart. For nerds. With a Chief of Staff.

You feel behind. Like way behind.

So you grab a shovel and start digging. A little hole over there to triage your inbox, one here to draft your tweets, one to check on those. Then you spend your day checking the holes are being dug right. Before long, you’re surrounded by holes and a mountain of dirt you gotta do something with.

Now as a man, holes are hardwired into my DNA. A few beers, a beach and a shovel, I’m digging a hole.

I’d take pride in it. I’d make the best one, impressively round, deep enough to see sea water seep through the bottom.

But I’d only dig one. There’s a whole beach but I chose this spot.

Next time the needy little nerd pings you: do you really want another hole?

Also, don’t dig big holes on the beach. They collapse.

kandidaty.zagolovok: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
kandidaty.tekst: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

kandidaty.zagolovok: TPU Model Design Considerations and Optimization Guide
kandidaty.tekst: The newly launched AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide provides hardware-grounded design rules to help developers maximize performance on TPUs for LLMs and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) workloads. Key principles include aligning reduction and output dimensions to 256 for systolic arrays, adopting LatentMoE to compress routed token traffic, and mapping parallel axes directly onto physical links.

kandidaty.zagolovok: Unlocking Stable On-Policy RL on TPU with Bitwise-Zero Train–Inference Mismatch
kandidaty.tekst: How we eliminated floating-point train–inference logprob drift for on-policy LLM reinforcement learning across 64 Cloud TPU v5p chips using a generalizable four-part JAX and Pallas recipe in Tunix.

kandidaty.zagolovok: Securing Your Agents: A Hands-On Guide to Agent Anomaly Detection
kandidaty.tekst: This guide walks developers through setting up Agent Anomaly Detection on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to monitor AI agent telemetry and catch behavioral risks. It demonstrates how to deploy a sample customer support agent, trigger out-of-scope security findings, and configure proactive alerts using Cloud Monitoring and Security Command Center.

hyped concepts this replaces:
- /goal
- "ultracode" / "ultra mode"
- "loop engineering"
- "agent to agent"
- "agent swarms"
- AI employees (see below)

my main aha moment is that you don't want "AI Employees", we do not have agi yet and you will just fail if you overpromise/overexpect. what you want is the "just" the next level of abstraction above single tasks, and the overwhelming consensus I've had talking to everyone at the frontier of agents (yes incl cog competitors) is agent managers that own outcomes. 

incidentally, as an employer of humans it's also how i distinguish between someone who "has agency" (owns a problem area, finds issues and researches/brings solutions not problems) and who doesn't (only does precisely what i asked, not proactive, doesn't come up with suggestions i didn't think about). guess which one i value more lol.

@testingcatalog: SGLang now runs on Amazon's AWS Trainium chips. Top labs like Meta and Google use this open-source software to run AI models.

It already supports NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Google chips, letting AI companies choose the chip that best fits their pipeline without switching software.

SGLang takes each request, runs the model on the chips, and sends the answer back to many users at once. It can also run image and video models like FLUX and Wan2.2.

Цитирует @sgl_project: 2,000+ people. Two days. The first SGLang Summit.

Together, we announced SGLang v1.0, released Miles v0.2, and launched the SGLang Consortium with nine founding members: @nvidia, @AMD, @intel, @Google, @Meta, @thinkymachines, @Cloudflare, @modal, and @radixark.

SGLang is now used by 332 organizations. At Meta, it powers production inference for products serving billions of users. Teams from Modal, Cloudflare, LinkedIn, and others shared their production lessons.

Across 90+ technical talks and six hands-on workshops, the community explored what comes next for inference, reinforcement learning, and AI agents.

To everyone building, deploying, and contributing: thank you for making this possible.

kandidaty.tekst:
@btibor91: I've been testing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on my day-to-day work

Most of what I gave them, small or bigger tasks, they got done - finding out why something broke, managing servers across multiple data centers, building new projects, fixing defects, reviewing changes, taking care of backups and monitoring

Also smaller tasks like research, admin and office work

During testing of GPT-6 Astra, it moved a nearly 20-year-old codebase from one version control system to another including the complete history 

This time I asked the new Astra to upgrade that same multimillion-line legacy app, with its legacy dependencies, from a very outdated version of its programming language to the current one

After about 3 hours I could already use it locally, and after about 6 hours all tests passed from a clean checkout

There's of course still more work to do, but the first results are very promising

I used them mostly in the Codex app and in T3 Code, which I now prefer for most of my work

T3 Code runs on my Mac, and I can connect to it from my Omarchy machine or from the iOS app over VPN and continue where I left off

I use Codex and Claude Code directly from T3 Code, so I can hand off between them and orchestrate subagents across both, because I use Astra together with Fable & Opus

I let one do the research and give its findings to the other to see what it missed, to brainstorm how to fix something or how to approach a problem

They also review each other's work - Astra still finds defects in Fable's code and Fable still finds defects in Astra's code

So it still makes sense to use both in my opinion, for me Astra and Fable are the best team currently available

Every new model works and communicates a bit differently than the one before, and so far adapting how I use it was enough for me to work well with it

Pro 200 gets Ultrafast for the first time (with Sol), and Pro 500 gets it with both Astra and Sol

Astra is also 20% cheaper in the API now - $8 input and $40 output per 1M tokens

For my work these are good models - I'll keep using Astra and move my other tasks to the new Sol
